claim: Listeners with hearing loss often struggle to understand speech in noise, even with a hearing aid.
source: Listeners with hearing loss often struggle to understand speech in noise, even with a hearing aid.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: Large-scale brain recordings were made from gerbils while presenting a large database of speech and noise sounds.
source: To better understand the auditory processing deficits that underlie this problem, we made large-scale brain recordings from gerbils, a common animal model for human hearing, while presenting a large database of speech and noise sounds.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The neural subspace in which speech is encoded is low-dimensional.
source: We first used manifold learning to identify the neural subspace in which speech is encoded and found that it is low-dimensional and that the dynamics within it are profoundly distorted by hearing loss.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the manifold learning analysis presented in the results.

claim: The dynamics within the neural subspace encoding speech are profoundly distorted by hearing loss.
source: We first used manifold learning to identify the neural subspace in which speech is encoded and found that it is low-dimensional and that the dynamics within it are profoundly distorted by hearing loss.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the manifold learning analysis comparing normal hearing and hearing loss animals.

claim: A deep neural network was trained to replicate the neural coding of speech with and without hearing loss.
source: We then trained a deep neural network (DNN) to replicate the neural coding of speech with and without hearing loss and analyzed the underlying network dynamics.
evidence: This describes the DNN modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Hearing loss primarily impacts spectral processing.
source: We found that hearing loss primarily impacts spectral processing, creating nonlinear distortions in cross-frequency interactions that result in a hypersensitivity to background noise that persists even after amplification with a hearing aid.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the DNN analysis of basic acoustic features.

claim: Hearing loss creates nonlinear distortions in cross-frequency interactions.
source: We found that hearing loss primarily impacts spectral processing, creating nonlinear distortions in cross-frequency interactions that result in a hypersensitivity to background noise that persists even after amplification with a hearing aid.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the DNN analysis of narrowband target and masker sounds.

claim: Hearing loss results in hypersensitivity to background noise that persists even after amplification with a hearing aid.
source: We found that hearing loss primarily impacts spectral processing, creating nonlinear distortions in cross-frequency interactions that result in a hypersensitivity to background noise that persists even after amplification with a hearing aid.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the DNN analysis of speech in noise with and without hearing aid amplification.

claim: Hearing loss is a widespread problem with far-reaching consequences ranging from lost productivity and social isolation to decreases in quality of life and mental health.
source: Hearing loss is a widespread problem with far-reaching consequences ranging from lost productivity and social isolation to decreases in quality of life and mental health (Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2017.

claim: Hearing loss imposes a growing societal burden with associated costs approaching $1 trillion annually.
source: It also imposes a growing societal burden with associated costs approaching $1 trillion annually (World Health Organization, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to World Health Organization, 2021.

claim: Hearing aids are the only widely available treatment for hearing loss.
source: Hearing aids are the only widely available treatment for hearing loss, but, unfortunately, current devices provide limited benefit in many workplace and social settings (Lesica, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and a citation to Lesica, 2018.

claim: Current hearing aids provide limited benefit in many workplace and social settings.
source: Hearing aids are the only widely available treatment for hearing loss, but, unfortunately, current devices provide limited benefit in many workplace and social settings (Lesica, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lesica, 2018.

claim: One common consequence of cochlear damage is a loss of sensitivity that renders low-intensity sounds inaudible.
source: One common consequence of cochlear damage is a loss of sensitivity that renders low-intensity sounds inaudible.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about hearing loss.

claim: Cochlear damage has consequences beyond lost sensitivity that cause many people to struggle with high-intensity sounds that are well above their audibility threshold.
source: But cochlear damage has other consequences beyond lost sensitivity that cause many people to struggle with high-intensity sounds that are well above their audibility threshold (Moore, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Moore, 2007.

claim: People with hearing loss often have difficulties understanding speech in noisy settings, with or without a hearing aid.
source: For example, people with hearing loss often have difficulties understanding speech in noisy settings, with or without a hearing aid (Larson et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Larson et al., 2000.

claim: The pathophysiology underlying high-intensity deficits in hearing loss remains poorly understood.
source: The pathophysiology underlying these high-intensity deficits remains poorly understood, and, as a result, they are largely ignored by clinicians and hearing aid designers.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: High-intensity deficits in hearing loss are largely ignored by clinicians and hearing aid designers.
source: The pathophysiology underlying these high-intensity deficits remains poorly understood, and, as a result, they are largely ignored by clinicians and hearing aid designers.
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical practice based on the lack of understanding.

claim: The consequences of cochlear damage for the processing of both low- and high-intensity sounds have been well described at the level of the auditory nerve.
source: The consequences of cochlear damage for the processing of both low- and high-intensity sounds have been well described at the level of the auditory nerve (AN; Young, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Young, 2008.

claim: Hearing loss causes a general decrease in neural activity resulting from lost sensitivity.
source: In addition to the general decrease in neural activity resulting from lost sensitivity, there are also complex changes in the spatiotemporal structure of the neural activity patterns that encode acoustic information, such as lost synchrony capture (Miller et al., 1997) and distorted tonotopy (Henry et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about auditory nerve responses.

claim: Hearing loss causes complex changes in the spatiotemporal structure of neural activity patterns, such as lost synchrony capture.
source: In addition to the general decrease in neural activity resulting from lost sensitivity, there are also complex changes in the spatiotemporal structure of the neural activity patterns that encode acoustic information, such as lost synchrony capture (Miller et al., 1997) and distorted tonotopy (Henry et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Miller et al., 1997.

claim: Hearing loss causes distorted tonotopy in the auditory nerve.
source: In addition to the general decrease in neural activity resulting from lost sensitivity, there are also complex changes in the spatiotemporal structure of the neural activity patterns that encode acoustic information, such as lost synchrony capture (Miller et al., 1997) and distorted tonotopy (Henry et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Henry et al., 2016.

claim: It has been difficult to differentiate between competing theories about how peripheral changes associated with hearing loss lead to perceptual deficits due to few explicit studies comparing neural coding in central auditory areas before and after hearing loss.
source: But, with few explicit studies comparing neural coding in central auditory areas before and after hearing loss, it has been difficult to differentiate between competing theories or to identify which peripheral changes are most important to address.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of research in the field.

claim: A recent study found that hearing loss and hearing aids impacted phoneme selectivity in individual neurons in the inferior colliculus.
source: One recent study of individual neurons in the inferior colliculus (IC) with and without hearing loss and hearing aids found that some properties, such as phoneme selectivity, were impacted while others, such as frequency selectivity and trial-to-trial variability, were not (Armstrong et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Armstrong et al., 2022.

claim: A recent study found that hearing loss and hearing aids did not impact frequency selectivity and trial-to-trial variability in individual neurons in the inferior colliculus.
source: One recent study of individual neurons in the inferior colliculus (IC) with and without hearing loss and hearing aids found that some properties, such as phoneme selectivity, were impacted while others, such as frequency selectivity and trial-to-trial variability, were not (Armstrong et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Armstrong et al., 2022.

claim: Neural coding in downstream areas such as the IC likely involves emergent network-level properties that are not readily apparent in the activity of individual neurons.
source: But, while characterizing the impact of hearing loss on neural coding in individual neurons may be sufficient at the level of the AN (a set of largely homogeneous fibers driven by a few thousand inner hair cells), neural coding in downstream areas such as the IC, which are much larger and more complex, likely involves emergent network-level properties that are not readily apparent in the activity of individual neurons.
evidence: This is a statement based on inference from the complexity of the IC compared to the AN.

claim: Manifold learning can be useful to find more compact representations of high-dimensional neural activity patterns that retain important features.
source: One of the challenges in characterizing neural coding at the network level is the high dimensionality of the activity patterns. If the goal is to gain insight into the underlying computations that the activity reflects, it can be useful to find more compact representations of the full activity that retain its important features. This process, often termed 'manifold learning' (Mitchell-Heggs et al., 2023; Williamson et al., 2019), typically utilizes techniques such as principal component analysis (PCA) that identify a projection of the full activity into a lower dimensional space that retains as much of its variance as possible.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mitchell-Heggs et al., 2023 and Williamson et al., 2019.

claim: Gerbils are a common animal model for the study of human hearing.
source: In this study, we use manifold learning to investigate the impact of hearing loss on the neural coding of speech in gerbils, a common animal model for the study of human hearing.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Large-scale intracranial recordings allow comprehensive sampling of activity from individual animals at fine spatial and temporal scales critical for encoding speech.
source: We employ large-scale intracranial recordings that allow us to achieve comprehensive sampling of activity from individual animals at the fine spatial and temporal scales that are critical for encoding speech (Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2013.

claim: Neurons in the IC can encode information about speech with millisecond temporal precision.
source: We processed the recordings to extract multi-unit activity (MUA) spike counts for each recording channel, using 1.3 ms time bins to account for the fact that neurons in the IC can encode information about speech with millisecond temporal precision (Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2013.

claim: Signal correlations in IC activity are dominated by features that are reproducible across repeated trials rather than features that vary from trial-to-trial.
source: Previous work has shown that the correlations in IC activity are dominated by 'signal' (features of activity that are reproducible across repeated trials and, thus, convey acoustic information) rather than 'noise' (features of activity that vary from trial-to-trial and reflect intrinsic noise or fluctuations in brain state) (Figure 1b; Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2013 and data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Signal variance accounted for only 40% of the overall variance in IC activity.
source: Signal correlations were also dominant in our recordings: although signal variance (the covariance in activity across repeated trials) accounted for only 40% of the overall variance in activity, signal correlations accounted for 95% of the total correlation between units (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of recorded neural activity shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Signal correlations accounted for 95% of the total correlation between units in IC recordings.
source: Signal correlations were also dominant in our recordings: although signal variance (the covariance in activity across repeated trials) accounted for only 40% of the overall variance in activity, signal correlations accounted for 95% of the total correlation between units (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of recorded neural activity shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Between 5 and 10 principal components were required to explain 95% of the signal variance in IC activity for normal hearing animals.
source: The signal variance explained saturated quickly, indicating that the signal dimensionality was much lower than the overall dimensionality, with only a small number of PCs (between 5 and 10) required to explain 95% of the signal variance in the original activity (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The signal dynamics from one normal hearing animal accounted for, on average, 96% of the variance in the signal dynamics from other normal hearing animals.
source: We found that the signal dynamics for different animals were remarkably similar, with the signal dynamics from one animal accounting for, on average, 96% of the variance in the signal dynamics from other animals (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-animal comparison shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss was induced in gerbils by exposing them to broadband noise using established protocols.
source: We induced sloping mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) by exposing gerbils (n = 6) to broadband noise using established protocols (Armstrong et al., 2022; Suberman et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental method for inducing hearing loss, supported by citations.

claim: Between 4 and 7 principal components were required to explain 95% of the signal variance in IC activity for animals with hearing loss.
source: The results for animals with hearing loss were similar to those for animals with normal hearing: the overall dimensionality of the neural activity was high (Figure 2f); the dimensionality of the signal manifold was low (Figure 2g; between 4 and 7 PCs required to explain 95% of the signal variance); and the signal dynamics were similar across animals (Figure 2h; 95% average variance explained), demonstrating again that the signal manifold is fundamental and robust.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the PCA analysis for hearing loss animals shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The signal dynamics for different animals with hearing loss were similar, with 95% average variance explained across animals.
source: The results for animals with hearing loss were similar to those for animals with normal hearing: the overall dimensionality of the neural activity was high (Figure 2f); the dimensionality of the signal manifold was low (Figure 2g; between 4 and 7 PCs required to explain 95% of the signal variance); and the signal dynamics were similar across animals (Figure 2h; 95% average variance explained), demonstrating again that the signal manifold is fundamental and robust.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-animal comparison for hearing loss animals shown in Figure 2h.

claim: The similarity between the signal dynamics of normal hearing animals and animals with hearing loss was 78% average variance explained.
source: But the similarity between the signal dynamics of normal hearing animals and animals with hearing loss was much lower than that between animals with the same hearing status (Figure 2h and i; 78% average variance explained).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-animal comparison between different hearing statuses shown in Figure 2h and i.

claim: The activity within the signal manifold of an animal with hearing loss is not linearly predictable from the activity within the signal manifold of a normal hearing animal.
source: This result indicates that the activity within the signal manifold of an animal with hearing loss is not linearly predictable from the activity within the signal manifold of a normal hearing animal and, thus, that the impact of hearing loss at the network level is a true nonlinear distortion that reshapes the neural code in a complex way.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low similarity between signal dynamics of normal hearing and hearing loss animals.

claim: The impact of hearing loss at the network level is a true nonlinear distortion that reshapes the neural code in a complex way.
source: This result indicates that the activity within the signal manifold of an animal with hearing loss is not linearly predictable from the activity within the signal manifold of a normal hearing animal and, thus, that the impact of hearing loss at the network level is a true nonlinear distortion that reshapes the neural code in a complex way.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low similarity between signal dynamics of normal hearing and hearing loss animals.

claim: The DNN's predictive power approached 100% for the units with highest explainable variance.
source: We trained and tested a separate DNN for each animal (after partitioning the recordings into training and test sets as described above) and found that they performed with remarkable accuracy. The explainable variance explained for activity in the test set approached 100% for the units with highest explainable variance and was far beyond that achieved by a standard single-layer linear–nonlinear model (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DNN performance evaluation shown in Figure 3c.

claim: DNN performance plateaued with more than eight channels in the bottleneck layer for both normal hearing animals and those with hearing loss.
source: We varied the size of the bottleneck layer and found that performance plateaued with more than eight channels for both normal hearing animals and those with hearing loss, consistent with the dimensionality of the signal manifold identified through PCA (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DNN architecture optimization shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The signal dynamics for animals with the same hearing status derived from DNNs were nearly identical, with 97% average variance explained for both normal hearing and hearing loss.
source: We also assessed the similarity of the DNN-derived signal dynamics across animals by measuring how much of the variance in the bottleneck activations from one animal could be explained by the bottleneck activations from another (Figure 3d and e; allowing for additional linear transformation). We found that the signal dynamics for animals with the same hearing status were nearly identical (97% average variance explained for both normal hearing and hearing loss), while the similarity between the signal dynamics for animals with normal hearing and those with hearing loss was much lower (87% average variance explained).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DNN-derived signal dynamics comparison shown in Figure 3d and e.

claim: The similarity between DNN-derived signal dynamics for animals with normal hearing and those with hearing loss was 87% average variance explained.
source: We found that the signal dynamics for animals with the same hearing status were nearly identical (97% average variance explained for both normal hearing and hearing loss), while the similarity between the signal dynamics for animals with normal hearing and those with hearing loss was much lower (87% average variance explained).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DNN-derived signal dynamics comparison shown in Figure 3d and e.

claim: DNNs trained on speech explained an average of 83% of the explainable variance in recorded responses to pure tones across animals.
source: To examine the degree to which the DNNs trained on speech were capable of predicting responses to other sounds, we compared recorded and DNN-generated responses to pure tones with different frequencies and intensities (Figure 3f). The DNNs performed well, explaining an average of 83% of the explainable variance in the recorded activity across animals.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DNN generalization test shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Transfer learning with frozen encoders explained an average of 85% of the explainable variance in responses to SAM noise for new animals.
source: We then used the new DNN model (the frozen encoder and the optimized readout) to predict responses from the new animal to sinusoidally amplitude modulated (SAM) broadband noise sounds with different modulation frequencies, modulation depths, and intensities. The new DNN models performed well, explaining an average of 85% of the explainable variance in the recorded activity across animals.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the transfer learning test shown in Figure 3g.

claim: For animals with hearing loss, the trajectories for different tone frequencies clustered into two groups, one for low frequencies and one for high frequencies.
source: For animals with hearing loss, the signal dynamics were dramatically different. At moderate intensity, only the lowest frequencies elicited any activation (as expected, given the larger elevation in intensity thresholds at high frequencies; Figure 2—figure supplement 1). At higher intensity, all tones elicited activation, but rather than forming an orderly arrangement within the manifold, the trajectories for different frequencies clustered into two groups, one for low frequencies and one for high frequencies.
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the signal dynamics analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for pure tones at the same moderate intensity was 0.59 ± 0.02.
source: Overall, the similarity between the RDMs for different normal hearing animals at moderate intensity (55 dB SPL) was high (0.91 ± 0.01; mean ± SEM; n = 15 pairwise comparisons; Figure 4f; for full details of all statistical tests, see Table 1). The similarity between the normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs at the same moderate intensity was much lower (0.59 ± 0.02; n = 36) and remained relatively low even at the best intensity (0.78 ± 0.02; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for pure tones at the best intensity was 0.78 ± 0.02.
source: The similarity between the normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs at the same moderate intensity was much lower (0.59 ± 0.02; n = 36) and remained relatively low even at the best intensity (0.78 ± 0.02; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The similarity between the dynamics for normal hearing and hearing loss animals for pure tones at the same moderate intensity after alignment via CCA was 0.37 ± 0.02.
source: Overall, the similarity between the dynamics for different normal hearing animals at moderate intensity after alignment via CCA was extremely high (0.98 ± 0.01; n = 15; Figure 4h). The similarity between the aligned dynamics for normal hearing and hearing loss animals at the same moderate intensity was much lower (0.37 ± 0.02; n = 36) and remained below normal even when compared at the best intensity (0.88 ± 0.01; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the CCA analysis shown in Figure 4h.

claim: The similarity between the dynamics for normal hearing and hearing loss animals for pure tones at the best intensity after alignment via CCA was 0.88 ± 0.01.
source: The similarity between the aligned dynamics for normal hearing and hearing loss animals at the same moderate intensity was much lower (0.37 ± 0.02; n = 36) and remained below normal even when compared at the best intensity (0.88 ± 0.01; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the CCA analysis shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Hearing loss results in a fundamental disruption of spectral processing at the network level.
source: Taken together, the RSA and CCA results suggest that hearing loss results in a fundamental disruption of spectral processing at the network level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RSA and CCA results for pure tones.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing RDMs for SAM noise at moderate intensity was 0.99 ± 0.01.
source: This was confirmed by RSA (Figure 5f), which indicated that while the similarity between normal hearing RDMs at moderate intensity (55 dB SPL) was extremely high (0.99 ± 0.01; n = 15), the similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs was lower (0.76 ± 0.01; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for SAM noise shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for SAM noise at the same moderate intensity was 0.76 ± 0.01.
source: This was confirmed by RSA (Figure 5f), which indicated that while the similarity between normal hearing RDMs at moderate intensity (55 dB SPL) was extremely high (0.99 ± 0.01; n = 15), the similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs was lower (0.76 ± 0.01; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for SAM noise shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for SAM noise at the best intensity was 0.99 ± 0.01.
source: But when compared at the best intensity to eliminate differences related to audibility, the dynamics for animals with hearing loss became nearly identical to those for animals with normal hearing (Figure 5e), and this was reflected in the similarity between RDMs (0.99 ± 0.01; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for SAM noise shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The similarity between the dynamics for normal hearing and hearing loss animals for SAM noise at the best intensity after alignment via CCA was 0.95 ± 0.01.
source: The similarity between the aligned dynamics for normal hearing and hearing loss animals was much lower when compared at the same moderate intensity (0.44 ± 0.02; n = 36) but increased to normal levels when the comparison was made at the best intensity (0.95 ± 0.01; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the CCA analysis for SAM noise shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Hearing loss has little impact on temporal processing beyond that which results from decreased audibility.
source: Thus, it appears that hearing loss has little impact on temporal processing beyond that which results from decreased audibility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SAM noise analysis results.

claim: Consonants vary widely in their spectral properties and are the primary contributor to the perceptual deficits exhibited by people with hearing loss when listening to ongoing speech.
source: We focused on consonants, which vary widely in their spectral properties and are the primary contributor to the perceptual deficits exhibited by people with hearing loss when listening to ongoing speech (Fogerty et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fogerty et al., 2012.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing RDMs for consonants in quiet at conversational intensity was 0.94 ± 0.01.
source: The differences in the dynamics for normal hearing animals and those with hearing loss were evident in the RDMs (Figure 6e). When compared at a typical conversational intensity (60 dB SPL), the similarity between normal hearing RDMs was high (0.94 ± 0.01; n = 15), but the similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs was low (0.23 ± 0.02; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for consonants in quiet shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for consonants in quiet at conversational intensity was 0.23 ± 0.02.
source: When compared at a typical conversational intensity (60 dB SPL), the similarity between normal hearing RDMs was high (0.94 ± 0.01; n = 15), but the similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs was low (0.23 ± 0.02; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for consonants in quiet shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for consonants in quiet at the best intensity was 0.87 ± 0.01.
source: The normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs were much more similar when compared at the best intensity, though some differences remained (0.87 ± 0.01; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for consonants in quiet shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for consonants in quiet with a hearing aid was 0.91 ± 0.01.
source: The frequency-dependent amplification was effective in reducing the distortion in the dynamics for animals with hearing loss. The overall similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss animals as measured by RSA was restored to normal levels (0.91 ± 0.01; n = 36; Figure 6e), and the similarity measured after alignment via CCA was also increased, though some residual distortion remained (0.86 ± 0.01; n = 36; Figure 6f).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for consonants in quiet with hearing aid shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss dynamics for consonants in quiet with a hearing aid after alignment via CCA was 0.86 ± 0.01.
source: The overall similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss animals as measured by RSA was restored to normal levels (0.91 ± 0.01; n = 36; Figure 6e), and the similarity measured after alignment via CCA was also increased, though some residual distortion remained (0.86 ± 0.01; n = 36; Figure 6f).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the CCA analysis for consonants in quiet with hearing aid shown in Figure 6f.

claim: For normal hearing animals, a decoder identified 55% of consonants correctly when presented at conversational intensity.
source: To evaluate the functional consequences of the remaining distortion, we turned to decoding. We trained a support vector machine to classify consonants based on the signal dynamics for each animal. For normal hearing animals, the decoder identified 55% of consonants correctly (±1%; n = 6; chance = 4.5%) when the consonants were presented at conversational intensity (Figure 6g).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis shown in Figure 6g.

claim: For animals with hearing loss, consonant decoding performance at conversational intensity was 41 ± 1%.
source: For animals with hearing loss, performance at the same intensity was lower (41 ± 1%; n = 6) but increased substantially at best intensity (47 ± 1%; n = 6), and increased further still with frequency-dependent amplification by the hearing aid (49 ± 1%; n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis shown in Figure 6g.

claim: For animals with hearing loss, consonant decoding performance at best intensity was 47 ± 1%.
source: For animals with hearing loss, performance at the same intensity was lower (41 ± 1%; n = 6) but increased substantially at best intensity (47 ± 1%; n = 6), and increased further still with frequency-dependent amplification by the hearing aid (49 ± 1%; n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis shown in Figure 6g.

claim: For animals with hearing loss, consonant decoding performance with a hearing aid was 49 ± 1%.
source: For animals with hearing loss, performance at the same intensity was lower (41 ± 1%; n = 6) but increased substantially at best intensity (47 ± 1%; n = 6), and increased further still with frequency-dependent amplification by the hearing aid (49 ± 1%; n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Amplification cannot completely restore the neural code for speech in quiet to normal, but the residual distortions are relatively minor.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that while amplification cannot completely restore the neural code for speech in quiet to normal, the residual distortions are relatively minor.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RSA, CCA, and decoding results for consonants in quiet.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing RDMs for consonants in noise at high intensity was 0.89 ± 0.02.
source: When compared at the same high intensity (70 dB SPL), typical of a social setting, both RSA and CCA indicated strong effects of hearing loss on the signal dynamics for speech in noise (Figure 7e and f). The similarity between normal hearing RDMs was high (0.89 ± 0.02; n = 15), but the similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs was much lower (0.15 ± 0.03; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for consonants in noise shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for consonants in noise at the same high intensity was 0.15 ± 0.03.
source: The similarity between normal hearing RDMs was high (0.89 ± 0.02; n = 15), but the similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs was much lower (0.15 ± 0.03; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for consonants in noise shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for consonants in noise at best intensity was 0.62 ± 0.02.
source: Amplification to best intensity increased the similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs (0.62 ± 0.02; n = 36), as did the frequency-weighted amplification provided by the hearing aid (0.56 ± 0.03; n = 36), but neither was sufficient to bring the similarity close to normal levels.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for consonants in noise shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs for consonants in noise with a hearing aid was 0.56 ± 0.03.
source: Amplification to best intensity increased the similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss RDMs (0.62 ± 0.02; n = 36), as did the frequency-weighted amplification provided by the hearing aid (0.56 ± 0.03; n = 36), but neither was sufficient to bring the similarity close to normal levels.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RSA analysis for consonants in noise shown in Figure 7e.

claim: For both forms of amplification, the similarity of the signal dynamics for speech in noise to those with normal hearing was much lower than for speech in quiet.
source: For both forms of amplification, the similarity of the signal dynamics for speech in noise to those with normal hearing was much lower than for speech in quiet (best intensity: 0.62 vs. 0.87, n = 36; p<1e-10, paired t-test; hearing aid: 0.56 vs. 0.91, n = 36, p<1e-10, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between speech in noise and speech in quiet results with statistical testing.

claim: For normal hearing animals, a decoder identified 32% of consonants correctly in noise.
source: Decoding the signal dynamics for each animal suggested that the distortions in the signal dynamics for speech in noise had functional consequences (Figure 7g). For normal hearing animals, the decoder identified 32% of consonants correctly (±1%; n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis for consonants in noise shown in Figure 7g.

claim: For animals with hearing loss, consonant decoding performance in noise at the same intensity was 15 ± 1%.
source: For animals with hearing loss, performance at the same intensity was lower (15 ± 1%; n = 6) and remained well below normal levels both at the best intensity (23 ± 1%; n = 6) or after processing with the hearing aid (22 ± 1%; n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis for consonants in noise shown in Figure 7g.

claim: For animals with hearing loss, consonant decoding performance in noise at best intensity was 23 ± 1%.
source: For animals with hearing loss, performance at the same intensity was lower (15 ± 1%; n = 6) and remained well below normal levels both at the best intensity (23 ± 1%; n = 6) or after processing with the hearing aid (22 ± 1%; n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis for consonants in noise shown in Figure 7g.

claim: For animals with hearing loss, consonant decoding performance in noise with a hearing aid was 22 ± 1%.
source: For animals with hearing loss, performance at the same intensity was lower (15 ± 1%; n = 6) and remained well below normal levels both at the best intensity (23 ± 1%; n = 6) or after processing with the hearing aid (22 ± 1%; n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis for consonants in noise shown in Figure 7g.

claim: For speech in quiet at best intensity, the correlation between normal hearing and hearing loss dynamics after projection onto the first canonical component was 0.94 ± 0.01.
source: When compared at best intensity (Figure 8a), there was good alignment between the dynamics for animals with normal hearing and hearing loss. The correlation for pairs of animals after projection onto the first CC, which accounted for 88 ± 2% and 71 ± 7% of the variance in animals with normal hearing (n = 6) and hearing loss (n = 6), respectively, was 0.94 ± 0.01 (n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MCCA analysis for speech in quiet shown in Figure 8a.

claim: For speech in quiet with a hearing aid, the correlation between normal hearing and hearing loss dynamics after projection onto the second canonical component was 0.73 ± 0.01.
source: With the hearing aid (Figure 8b), the alignment between the dynamics for animals with normal hearing and hearing loss was even better. The correlation after projection onto the first CC remained high (0.94 ± 0.01; n = 36) and the correlation after projection onto the second CC rose substantially (0.73 ± 0.01; n = 36).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MCCA analysis for speech in quiet with hearing aid shown in Figure 8b.

claim: For speech in noise, the first canonical component accounted for 56 ± 1% of the variance for normal hearing animals but only 38 ± 7% for animals with hearing loss.
source: But even for the first two CCs for which the alignment was relatively good, the percent of the variance accounted for by each was substantially different for normal hearing animals and those with hearing loss. The first CC, which provided a clean reflection of each consonant, accounted for 56 ± 1% of the variance for normal hearing animals (n = 6), but only 38 ± 7% of the variance for animals with hearing loss (n = 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MCCA analysis for speech in noise shown in Figure 8c.

claim: For speech in noise, the second canonical component accounted for 28 ± 1% of the variance for normal hearing animals but 41 ± 6% for animals with hearing loss.
source: Conversely, the second CC, which was dominated by the background noise, accounted for 41 ± 6% of the variance for animals with hearing loss (n = 6), but only 28 ± 1% of the variance for animals with normal hearing.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MCCA analysis for speech in noise shown in Figure 8c.

claim: The balance of variance between neural subspaces encoding speech and background noise is tilted much more toward background noise in animals with hearing loss.
source: Thus, while the neural subspaces encoding the speech and the background noise seem to be similar for all animals, the balance of variance between these subspaces is tilted much more toward background noise in animals with hearing loss.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MCCA results for speech in noise.

claim: Hearing loss allows the signal dynamics to be captured by background noise at the expense of foreground speech in a way that cannot be corrected by simple frequency-dependent amplification.
source: Thus, it appears that hearing loss allows the signal dynamics to be captured by background noise at the expense of foreground speech in a way that cannot be corrected by simple frequency-dependent amplification.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MCCA results for speech in noise with hearing aid.

claim: For animals with normal hearing, the correlation between target only and target plus masker dynamics ranged from 0.25 to 0.75, with the masker having the largest impact when its center frequency was similar to that of the target.
source: For animals with normal hearing, the correlation between the target only and target plus masker dynamics ranged from 0.25 to 0.75, with the masker having the largest impact when its center frequency was similar to that of the target (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the narrowband target and masker analysis shown in Figure 8f.

claim: When compared at the same high intensity, the correlation for animals with hearing loss was typically lower than normal when the masker center frequency was low, especially when the target center frequency was high.
source: When compared at the same high intensity (70 dB SPL), the correlation for animals with hearing loss was typically lower than normal when the masker center frequency was low, especially when the target center frequency was high (Figure 8g).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the narrowband target and masker analysis shown in Figure 8g.

claim: Hearing loss creates deficits in spectral processing that manifest as highly nonlinear distortions in cross-frequency interactions that are particularly problematic for real-world speech in noise and cannot be corrected by simply compensating for lost sensitivity.
source: Thus, hearing loss appears to create deficits in spectral processing that manifest as highly nonlinear distortions in cross-frequency interactions that are particularly problematic for real-world speech in noise and cannot be corrected by simply compensating for lost sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the narrowband target and masker analysis results.

claim: Changes in spectral processing, particularly in the interactions between different frequencies, are the primary problem caused by hearing loss.
source: Our results suggest that changes in spectral processing, particularly in the interactions between different frequencies, are the primary problem.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from all the experimental results.

claim: Impaired spectral processing for simple tones does not appear to be a major problem for the neural coding of speech per se as suitable amplification corrected many of the distortions caused by hearing loss for speech in quiet.
source: While impaired spectral processing was evident for simple tones as a clustering of dynamical trajectories within the signal manifold, this impairment does not appear to be a major problem for the neural coding of speech per se as suitable amplification corrected many of the distortions caused by hearing loss for speech in quiet.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the results for tones and speech in quiet.

claim: The results are consistent with a recent study that found that hearing loss caused the IC activity patterns elicited by different phonemes to become less distinct, and that a hearing aid failed to correct this problem for speech in noise.
source: These results are consistent with a recent study that found that hearing loss caused the IC activity patterns elicited by different phonemes to become less distinct, and that a hearing aid failed to correct this problem for speech in noise (Armstrong et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Armstrong et al., 2022.

claim: Listeners with hearing loss struggle to combine temporal envelope cues across frequency channels.
source: They are also consistent with a body of work demonstrating that listeners with hearing loss struggle to combine temporal envelope cues across frequency channels (Healy and Bacon, 2002; Healy and Carson, 2010; Souza and Boike, 2006; Grant et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: When speech is reduced to a single amplitude-modulated band, speech recognition performance is similar for all listeners, independent of their hearing status.
source: When speech is reduced to a single amplitude-modulated band, speech recognition performance is similar for all listeners, independent of their hearing status, suggesting that temporal processing of the speech envelope per se is unaffected by hearing loss.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from perceptual studies.

claim: As additional amplitude-modulated bands are added to speech, performance increases more for normal hearing listeners than for those with hearing loss.
source: But as additional amplitude-modulated bands are added, performance increases more for normal hearing listeners than for those with hearing loss, suggesting that the latter group are less able to make use of complementary temporal information across multiple frequency channels.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from perceptual studies.

claim: The difference in speech recognition performance is most pronounced when comparing the ability to make use of temporal modulations in high-frequency channels (4–6 kHz) in the presence of temporal modulations in lower frequency channels (1–2 kHz).
source: This difference is most pronounced when comparing the ability to make use of temporal modulations in high-frequency channels (4–6 kHz) in the presence of temporal modulations in lower frequency channels (1–2 kHz) (Grant et al., 2007), and it does not appear to be a simple consequence of broadened frequency tuning but rather a specific deficit in cross-frequency interactions (Healy and Carson, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grant et al., 2007 and Healy and Carson, 2010.

claim: After hearing loss, the tuning curve 'tip' becomes less sensitive and may shift toward lower frequencies while the 'tail' may become more sensitive.
source: After hearing loss, the tuning curve 'tip' (corresponding to the characteristic frequency [CF] to which the fiber is most sensitive) becomes less sensitive and may shift toward lower frequencies while the 'tail' (corresponding to frequencies below CF) may become more sensitive (Young, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Young, 2012.

claim: In animals with mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss, auditory nerve fibers with high CFs responded excessively to low-frequency sounds.
source: One recent study has provided insight into how the complex spectral distortions in the cochlea impact the neural coding of speech in noise in the AN (Parida and Heinz, 2022). In animals with mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss, fibers with high CFs responded excessively to low-frequency sounds and it was this effect (rather than changes in frequency selectivity per se or temporal processing) that appeared to be most responsible for the disrupted neural coding of speech in noise.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Parida and Heinz, 2022.

claim: The distortion of spectral processing observed as clustering of network dynamics for simple tones in the IC does not appear to be present in the AN.
source: The distortion of spectral processing that we observe as clustering of network dynamics for simple tones in the IC, however, does not appear to be present in the AN. It is difficult to be certain since no directly comparable analysis has been performed on experimental AN responses, but our analysis of simulated AN responses suggests that hearing loss has more complex effects on the signal dynamics in the AN than simply causing clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from analysis of simulated AN responses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Animals with hearing loss displayed behavioral hypersensitivity for detection of tones at the edge frequencies around which the hearing loss increased from mild to moderate.
source: Distorted spectral processing has also recently been observed in the auditory cortex after mild-to-moderate sloping sensorineural hearing loss (McGill et al., 2022). Animals displayed behavioral hypersensitivity for detection of tones at the edge frequencies around which the hearing loss increased from mild to moderate as well as an overrepresentation of these frequencies in the cortical tonotopic map of BF.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to McGill et al., 2022.

claim: Some cortical neurons tuned to edge frequencies exhibited increased neural gain and synchrony after hearing loss.
source: Some cortical neurons tuned to these edge frequencies exhibited increased neural gain and synchrony, and direct stimulation of thalamocortical afferents demonstrated that hearing loss caused an increase in gain within the local cortical circuit.
evidence: This statement is based on findings from McGill et al., 2022.

claim: The complex suprathreshold effects of hearing loss present a difficult challenge for hearing aid designers.
source: The complex suprathreshold effects of hearing loss that are evident in the distorted neural signal dynamics observed in this study present a difficult challenge for hearing aid designers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about the complexity of hearing loss effects.

claim: Current hearing aids compensate for changes in the threshold and dynamic range of auditory processing using a framework built around a bank of bandpass filters with automatic gain control.
source: Current hearing aids compensate for changes in the threshold and dynamic range of auditory processing using a framework built around a bank of bandpass filters with automatic gain control.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about hearing aid design.

claim: It is difficult to imagine how current hearing aid frameworks could be used to compensate for problems such as hypersensitivity to background noise that involve highly nonlinear interactions across frequency bands.
source: The signal processing that can be performed by such a framework is highly constrained, and it is difficult to imagine how it could be used to compensate for problems such as hypersensitivity to background noise that involve highly nonlinear interactions across frequency bands.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current hearing aid technology and the findings of the study.

claim: Recent research on speech enhancement via DNNs has demonstrated the potential to yield dramatic improvements in performance.
source: Recent research on speech enhancement via DNNs has demonstrated the potential to yield dramatic improvements in performance (Wang, 2017; Luo and Mesgarani, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wang, 2017 and Luo and Mesgarani, 2019.

claim: Deep denoising may prove effective in situations with a single talker where it is obvious which sound is of interest.
source: This 'deep denoising' may prove effective in situations with a single talker where it is obvious which sound is of interest.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential application of deep denoising.

claim: There are many significant technical challenges that must be overcome before cognitive control of speech enhancement can be widely applied.
source: It may be possible to implement cognitive control to direct enhancement toward the sound of interest but there are many significant technical challenges that must be overcome before this approach can be widely applied (Geirnaert et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Geirnaert et al., 2021.

claim: It should be possible to identify optimal processing algorithms for hearing aids empirically by providing DNNs with the data they need to learn how best to transform sounds in order to elicit normal neural activity from an impaired auditory system.
source: A more flexible alternative is to identify optimal processing algorithms for hearing aids empirically by providing DNNs with the data they need to learn how best to transform sounds in order to elicit normal neural activity from an impaired auditory system (Lesica, 2018; Drakopoulos and Verhulst, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lesica, 2018 and Drakopoulos and Verhulst, 2022.

claim: The vast majority of people with hearing loss have only mild-to-moderate cochlear damage.
source: But the vast majority of people with hearing loss have only mild-to-moderate cochlear damage (Wilson et al., 2017), and there should be sufficient functionality remaining within the auditory system for a hearing aid to leverage when attempting elicit the necessary patterns of neural activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2017.

claim: Current models of the cochlea can faithfully capture the transformation of incoming sound into basilar membrane motion and AN activity.
source: Current models of the sensory periphery can be highly accurate. For example, there are numerous models of the cochlea that faithfully capture the transformation of incoming sound into basilar membrane motion and AN activity (Saremi et al., 2016; Verhulst et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Saremi et al., 2016 and Verhulst et al., 2018.

claim: Models of sensory processing in the brain have generally been much less accurate than models of the sensory periphery.
source: Models of sensory processing in the brain, however, have generally been much less accurate, with even the best models missing out on a significant fraction of the explainable variance in subcortical and cortical neural activity (Williamson et al., 2016; Rahman et al., 2020; McFarland et al., 2013; Vintch et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A DNN trained to replicate an established model of the cochlea provided accurate and generalizable predictions of the model's response to speech and tones.
source: Initial efforts to use DNNs to model the sensory periphery have shown that they can be as accurate as hand-designed biophysical models. In one recent study, a DNN trained to replicate an established model of the cochlea provided accurate and generalizable predictions of the model's response to speech and tones (Baby et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Baby et al., 2021.

claim: A DNN trained on retinal ganglion cell activity predicted nearly all of the explainable variance in responses to natural images.
source: In another study, a DNN trained on retinal ganglion cell activity predicted nearly all of the explainable variance in responses to natural images (Maheswaranathan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Maheswaranathan et al., 2019.

claim: DNN models of V1 responses to natural images explained 50 and 80% of the explainable variance in single-unit spike counts and calcium activity, respectively.
source: DNN models of V1 responses to natural images explained 50 and 80% of the explainable variance in single-unit spike counts and calcium activity, respectively (Cadena et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2019), while DNN models of V4 explained 90% of the explainable variance in multi-unit spike counts (Bashivan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cadena et al., 2019, Walker et al., 2019, and Bashivan et al., 2019.

claim: DNN models of A1 responses to speech and other natural sounds explain much of the explainable variance in high-gamma activity, fMRI voxel responses, or time-varying spike rates.
source: DNN models of A1 responses to speech and other natural sounds perform similarly well, explaining much of the explainable variance in high-gamma activity, fMRI voxel responses, or time-varying spike rates (Keshishian et al., 2020; Kell et al., 2018; Pennington and David, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Keshishian et al., 2020, Kell et al., 2018, and Pennington and David, 2022.

claim: The DNN models in this study simulate neural activity with full temporal resolution, capturing spike times with millisecond precision.
source: Our results improve on these initial successes in several important ways. Firstly, our models simulate neural activity with full temporal resolution, that is, spike times with millisecond precision.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the DNN models developed in this study.

claim: The activity produced by the DNN models is nearly indistinguishable from that recorded experimentally, capturing more than 95% of the explainable variance in many cases.
source: Secondly, the activity produced by our models is nearly indistinguishable from that recorded experimentally, capturing more than 95% of the explainable variance in many cases.
evidence: This describes the high accuracy of the DNN models developed in this study.

claim: The use of a low-dimensional bottleneck in the DNN allows for high performance within a framework that also provides a compact and interpretable description of the latent dynamics.
source: Finally, our use of a low-dimensional bottleneck allows us to achieve this performance within a framework that also provides a compact and interpretable description of the latent dynamics that underlie the full network activity patterns.
evidence: This describes a key methodological advantage of the DNN approach used in this study.

claim: It should now be possible to use computational models of the brain for exploratory basic research, with benefits that are both scientific and ethical.
source: With these advances, it should now be possible to use computational models of the brain for exploratory basic research, with benefits that are both scientific (studies are no longer data limited) and ethical (animal experiments can be limited to confirmatory studies), as well as for technology development (such as improved hearing aids, as described above).
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential applications of the DNN modeling approach.

claim: With further effort, it may be possible to build models that not only simulate but also mirror the underlying structure of biological systems.
source: With further effort, it may be possible to build models that are not only black-box simulators but also mirror the underlying structure of biological systems (Jazayeri and Ostojic, 2021; Chung and Abbott, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jazayeri and Ostojic, 2021 and Chung and Abbott, 2021.

claim: Experiments were performed on 12 young-adult gerbils of both sexes.
source: Experiments were performed on 12 young-adult gerbils of both sexes that were born and raised in standard laboratory conditions.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Six of the animals were exposed to noise when they were 16–18 weeks old.
source: Six of the animals were exposed to noise when they were 16–18 weeks old.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for inducing hearing loss.

claim: ABR recordings and large-scale IC recordings were made from all animals when they were 20–24 weeks old.
source: ABR recordings and large-scale IC recordings were made from all animals when they were 20–24 weeks old.
evidence: This describes the timing of the neural recordings.

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by the UK Home Office.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by the UK Home Office (PPL P56840C21).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the experiments.
